lesson.title: Don't Stop Halfway: Factoring Every Layer of an Expression
lesson.summary: Factoring completely means applying every applicable technique, greatest common factor first, then trinomial or special patterns, until no remaining factor can be broken down any further.
lesson.body:
Factoring completely means continuing to factor an expression until every remaining factor is prime, meaning none of them can be split further using integer coefficients. This usually requires combining more than one technique in a fixed order, because a single method rarely finishes the job on its own. The reliable order is: pull out the greatest common factor first, then look at what remains and check whether it is a difference of squares, a perfect square trinomial, or a general trinomial that factors into two binomials.

Consider 3x^3 - 12x. The first step is always to look for a GCF. Both terms share a factor of 3x, since 3x^3 = 3x times x^2 and 12x = 3x times 4. Pulling that out gives 3x(x^2 - 4). At this point it would be tempting to stop, but the expression inside the parentheses, x^2 - 4, is itself a difference of squares, since x^2 is a perfect square and 4 = 2^2. A difference of squares a^2 - b^2 always factors as (a - b)(a + b), so x^2 - 4 factors as (x - 2)(x + 2). Putting it all together, the complete factorization is 3x(x - 2)(x + 2). To check this, multiply it back out. First (x - 2)(x + 2) = x^2 + 2x - 2x - 4 = x^2 - 4. Then 3x(x^2 - 4) = 3x^3 - 12x, which matches the original expression exactly.

A second example shows how the GCF step combines with trinomial factoring instead of a special pattern. Consider 2x^3 + 6x^2 - 8x. Every term shares a factor of 2x, so pulling it out gives 2x(x^2 + 3x - 4). The trinomial inside the parentheses factors by finding two integers that multiply to -4 and add to 3: those integers are 4 and -1, since 4 times -1 = -4 and 4 + (-1) = 3. So x^2 + 3x - 4 = (x + 4)(x - 1), and the complete factorization is 2x(x + 4)(x - 1). Multiplying back confirms it: 2x times (x^2 + 3x - 4) = 2x^3 + 6x^2 - 8x, matching the original expression.

The reason the GCF has to come first is practical: skipping it can hide the pattern that makes the rest of the factoring possible, or it can leave you factoring a trinomial with much larger, harder-to-find integer pairs than necessary. For example, trying to factor 3x^3 - 12x as a whole without removing 3x first offers no clean pattern to spot at all, since it is not a binomial that fits the difference of squares and not a trinomial that fits the usual ac-method.

This concept pulls together three separate skills, factoring by GCF, factoring trinomials, and factoring the difference of squares, into a single decision process applied to one expression, sometimes more than once if the resulting factors can themselves be factored again. A polynomial is only completely factored when every single factor left is prime: no common factor remains to pull out, and no factor can be split into two lower-degree polynomials with integer coefficients.

A common error is stopping after the first successful technique. Always ask, after each factoring step, whether any of the newly produced factors can be factored again before calling the work finished.
